newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Koreans raise millions for hungry compatriots.
newsitem.headline: South Koreans raise millions for hungry compatriots.

text.p: Images of hungry North Korean children have sparked an outpouring of public sympathy in South Korea, and ordinary citizens are digging into their pockets to raise millions of dollars for food aid.
The plight of South Korea's impoverished communist neighbour has struck a chord among all sectors of society.
As the enormity of the crisis hits home, church-goers are being urged to skip one meal each week and donate the savings to their brethren across the border.
The rush to stave off human catastrophe has pushed aside memories of a North Korean submarine incursion last year that provoked rage and fear among stunned South Koreans.

"After the submarine infiltration, the donations stopped," said Rhee Jong-geun, spokesman for the South Korean Red Cross, the only authorised channel for aid to the North. "But now the money is pouring in."
Red Cross offices have been inundated with letters stuffed with cash from students, housewives and old people.
Last week, the Red Cross shipped $1 million worth of food and vegetable seed to North Korea.
Christian groups are at the forefront of fund-raising activities. South Korea boasts some of the biggest -- and richest -- churches in the world.
On Tuesday the Korea Sharing Movement, which embraces religious and civic organisations, launched an ambitious plan to raise 17 billion won ($19 million) over two months.
To meet its goal, church pastors are urging their congregations to miss a meal each week. Also planned are charity concerts and street collections.

An umbrella organisation for militant groups advocating Korean unification is set to launch a drive for two billion won. The group includes the Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, which has half a million members.
On Wednesday it set up a table with cash boxes and plastered photographs of starving North Korean children on a pavement in a fashionable Seoul district.
"Citizens of Korea, you can save our bretheren North Koreans if you only donate the money you spend on a pack of cigarettes or a cup of coffee," a group activist bellowed through a loudhailer.
"Media reports have helped boost interest in the food crisis in the North," said Park Hong-soon, a leader of the so-called Love For Our Compatriots Pan-National Movement.
Ko Jung-sook, 70, dug through her handbag and pulled out 10,000 won ($11).
"If we don't save our bretheren, who will?" asked the elderly woman, who said she was born in the North and abandoned six siblings as she fled south during the 1950-53 Korean War.
"They could avoid famine if only we gave them the food we casually throw away."

Aid groups say public sentiment towards North Korea has shifted since Pyongyang publicly apologised last December for the intrusion by one of its submarines, which landed 26 armed agents on a South Korean beach.
Twenty four of the commandos were shot and killed, one was captured and one was never found.
Not all South Koreans are happy about sending food to a country that still threatens the South with its million-strong army and missiles.
"Occasionally some people will call to tell us we shouldn't be sending aid to an enemy which is still planning a war," said Rhee at the Red Cross.
(Conversion: $1 = 894)
